<reason>Both sides argued at a high level with disciplined, closed-book grounding and genuine progression. B (PRO) set the controlling frame first — what a marginal public dollar buys, not the average degree-holder's return — and A largely had to fight inside it, which gave B structural advantage. B then converted that frame into a repeated, easy-to-apply asymmetry (failed apprenticeship = paid year plus reference; failed subsidy = unfinished transcript plus non-dischargeable debt) and handled A's pressure questions with unusual candor: naming concrete employer sectors, conceding that only a minority of apprentices later earn a BA, and refusing to invent a completion number while noting A could not supply one either ("only one of us needs the estimate to be favorable"). A landed the best single counterpunch of the debate — the dilemma that apprenticeship "scales either small or bad," plus the reframe that B's "one link" is really three (the firm must teach, the skill must survive automation, the worker must be retained above training wages) — and A's closing correctly pushed back that a downside floor is not the same as higher long-run growth. But A's key repair, that subsidies rescue persistence rather than merely buy entry, arrived as assertion under direct pressure and was paired with an expected-value move that partially conceded B's central empirical claim about the marginal enrollee. B's answer to the scaling dilemma ("design is the proposition, stated fully") is somewhat convenient on magnitude, yet it is a live answer, whereas A's completion story remained the weaker of the two conditional chains after the exchange. Narrow but real edge to B for owning the frame, absorbing pressure honestly, and making the decision rule simpler.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Q1 demanding the marginal-completion number, followed by A's honest refusal and pivot to expected value plus persistence-rescue: A's reply was candid and partly effective, but it conceded the core empirical uncertainty B needed, letting B recast CON's case as a multiplied chain of probabilities against a bounded-downside alternative. A's strongest counter — "scales either small or bad" and "your one link is three links" — narrowed the gap but did not fully neutralize it.</best_rebuttal>
